cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a traditional Hawaiian feather cape (kīpuka) made of ʻapapane, ʻiʻiwi, ōʻō and chicken feathers on olonā matting — a garment distinctive of Native Hawaiian culture.

physical.title: cape
physical.summary:
Kipuka (cape), trapezoidal in shape, consisting of white, black and golden-brown chicken feathers as well as red ʻapapane feathers, some red ʻiʻiwi feathers and yellow ōʻō feathers, still attached to bird skin.  
The upper panel of the kipuka is comprised of a layer of olonā matting, onto which bird skins with feathers attached have been stitched. The feathers are mostly red (likely ʻapapane) with a row of yellow feathers, also on bird skins (possibly ōʻō or mamo) along the bottom edge of the mat.  
The lower part of the kipuka consists of a central panel of white chicken feathers, many of which have been trimmed so the feather ends in two points. There are bands of black chicken feathers above and below the central panel and broad bands of golden-brown chicken feathers on either side. The feathers are tied in bundles to a groundwork of olonā fibre nae (net).  
Both the mat and nae are tied to a thick plaited olonā fibre cord that runs along the top of the kipuka and a thinner cord that runs along the sides. At the corners of the neckline the cords are plaited together and extend beyond the neckline to become ties. At the bottom of the kipuka the cords turn back on themselves and create loops.

cultural.vision_reason: Feather cape ('ahu'ula fragment) made of 'i'iwi and mamo feathers on olonā fiber netting — a classic Native Hawaiian chiefly garment.

physical.title: cape
physical.summary:
Cape (possibly a section of an ‘ahu’ula) made of red 'i'iwi and yellow mamo feathers (possibly some yellow ʻōʻō feathers) attached in bundles to an olonā fibre nae (net). The cape is shallowly curved and has a wide, almost straight, neckline and short collars.  
Yellow feathers are arranged into a band of seven niho (triangles) pointing up to the neckline along the top of the cape. Beneath them are two yellow loops and a band of yellow runs along the edge of the cape. The rest of the cape is red. Some of the yellow feathers have been trimmed to give a crisp edge between the yellow and red sections.  
The feathers are attached to the olonā nae in bundles. A plaited olonā fibre cord runs along the neckline and collars; the cords extend beyond the neckline where they taper and end in a knot. On the proper right there is a piece of kapa (barkcloth) tied to the end of the cord. The plaited olonā cords also extend slightly below the collar where they are cut short.  
The edge of the nae is roughly cut in places, with the bottom edge of the nae extending past the feathers in some areas.

cultural.vision_reason: This is a classic feathered 'ahu'ula (cape) made of red 'i'iwi and yellow mamo/'ō'ō feathers attached to an olonā fibre net, a garment form uniquely associated with Native Hawaiian chiefly regalia.

physical.title: cape
physical.summary:
Cape (possibly a section of an ‘ahu’ula) made of red 'i'iwi feathers and yellow mamo and ʻōʻō feathers attached in bundles to an olonā fibre nae (net). The cape is curved but mostly flat at the bottom edge and has a wide, almost straight, neckline.  
The red 'i'iwi feathers make up the main colour of the cape. The yellow feathers are arranged into a small hoaka (crescent) at the centre top of the cape. Two curved niho (triangles) of yellow sit at the collar and narrow towards the centre of the cape where they connect. Some of the yellow feathers have been trimmed to give a crisp edge between the yellow and red sections. Alternating bundles of red and yellow feathers are arranged along the neckline. The colour of the feathers varies slightly across the cape; a square section on the centre left of the cape may have faded, possibly due to light exposure. The colour and shape of the yellow feathers varies across the cape, with some sections containing long fluffy and pale coloured feathers and other sections more vibrant and less fluffy feathers.  
The feathers are attached to a very fine olonā nae in bundles. The bottom edge of the nae has possibly been cut short and some remnants of feather bundles are visible along the edge. A plaited olonā fibre cord runs along the neckline and collars. The cords extend beyond the neckline, creating ties for fastening the cape. The plaited olonā cords also extend below the collar, where they are folded back on themselves to create loops.
